SearchAliases: five positions of lord and minister
Senses.Explanation: In Caodong technical discourse, lord and minister name a relational configuration used to explain upright and inclined positions and their interaction. Caoshan Benji maps lord to the upright position and minister to the inclined, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister accord. A later Caoshan quotation repeats that mapping. Juelang Daosheng equates arriving within both with lord and minister according. Yinqian identifies the Caodong house through their accord. Langting Ting disputes the later classification of Caoshan's answers as five lord-and-minister positions. Shixi Xinyue sets the five positions beside Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Shaoyuan says the five positions are all penetrated when host and guest accord. These uses establish a technical relational family while preserving disagreement about its historical systematization.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,052 hits in 239 files and 235 works. Seven witnesses across seven independent works meet the packet floor and cover foundational mapping, repetition, final relation, school identification, historical dispute, house comparison, and penetration claim.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary ethical and political lists, the same graphs name the social relation of lord and minister. Hansong Zhicao and Gumei Dinglie place their proper duty beside affection between parent and child, distinctions between spouses, age order, and trust among friends. This coordinate-list grammar identifies political roles rather than the Caodong position system.
Senses.Note: Two explicit witnesses from two independent works establish the ordinary social-role sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 君臣道合事如何
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (明覺聰禪師語錄). Exact actor: the unnamed monk. An unnamed monk asks Mingjue Cong about ruler-and-minister accord.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 僧問 introduces both headword-bearing parallel lines and the later question; Mingjue Cong answers only after 師云.

Senses.Explanation: Ruler and minister accord names a relation in which differentiated positions function together. Langting Jingting glosses it with “one virtue, one mind,” and Zhe’an Fan places it beside concord among brothers. Chushi Fanqi answers the direct question with “together.” Ruibai Mingxue sets the accord aside to demand a turning phrase, while Langya Huijue says that even an ordered realm with calm seas remains beside the dharma body. The records use political coordination as a relational model and then publicly test whether it exhausts the matter.

Senses.Note: Exact count: 47 hits in 33 allowlisted texts. Family research covered the woodcutter, rotted axe/handle, chess game, lost road, Lanke person, and the separate Mount Lanke place-name. The allusion and the mountain are different referents and are split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 斧爛柯銷局未闌天風吹鶴下瑤壇
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben, in (天目中峰廣錄) (Extensive Record of Zhongfeng at Tianmu), says the handle is gone while the game remains unfinished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已有爛柯樵子本傳。前頌雪峯末後句。亦有挂樹壺公本傳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong Xingxiu, in (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄) (Wansong's Commentary in the Book of Serenity), identifies the original Lanke woodcutter account.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去，空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Senses.Note: Mount Lanke occurs as a compound place-name in several allowlisted texts. One exact place witness is sufficient to establish the distinct referent; the entry makes no claim about the mountain's outside history.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爛柯山雨似傾盆，龜嶺峯額頭汗出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiatang Huiyuan, in (瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄) (Extensive Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan), names rain on Mount Lanke.

Senses.Explanation: The same graph pair also forms the proper place-name Mount Lanke. Xiatang Huiyuan says that rain on Mount Lanke pours like a basin while Turtle Ridge's forehead sweats. This geographic referent is not the rotted axe handle or its woodcutter, even though the place-name inherits the same graphs; it therefore has its own sense.
